subtopic: MR. DIEFENBAKER    STATEMENT IN DEBATE BY MEMBER FOR VILLENEUVE

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: MR. DIEFENBAKER    STATEMENT IN DEBATE BY MEMBER FOR VILLENEUVE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise at once on a question of privilege arising out of a statement made yesterday afternoon by the hon. member for Villeneuve as recorded on page 5158 of Hansard. I was in the house when he commenced his remarks, but I was called out and was not present when he made these remarks, so it was not until this morning that I observed the statement. I quote from the translation at page 5158:
Mr. Speaker, that is nothing new for the Leader of the Opposition, since he stated in the past that family allowances were merely a piece of legislation to assist French Canadians in the province of Quebec. But I realized myself that in western Canada, and in the riding of the Leader of the Opposition, there were as many large families as there are in the province of Quebec.
Another point on which the Leader of the Opposition was wrong is that some years ago he was against family allowances because, he said, they were designed to help families in the province of Quebec.
Sir, there is not one vestige of truth in the suggestion that I, at any time, any place or under any circumstances, inside this house or outside, ever made the allegation or statement or any statement from which such inferences could be drawn. I want to make that clear now so that it will not be quoted later as not having been clearly denied.
Furthermore, as to the allegation that I was against family allowances, I simply recall to the attention of the house that when this matter was before parliament I was at one time alone in my support of family allowances: I stood for them knowing what the advantages were. Later on the entire party, with one exception, voted in favour of family allowances. I wanted to make these two points very clearly, and to state that the hon. gentleman's statement is unequivocally untrue.

subtopic: TEACHERS' SALARIES, NATIONAL DEFENCE
TEACHERS' SALARIES, NATIONAL DEFENCE
speechtext:
What are the salary schedules for teachers employed by Department of National Defence including a job description for each level?
Answer: In Canada, teachers are employed in dependants schools in Canada by a contract negotiated between the teacher and the official trustee of the school board at each defence base. In accordance with the regulations and orders governing the operation of

these schools the salary schedules for staff members shall be on a parity with those of comparable civilian operated schools in the area. A supporting statement to this effect shall be obtained from the local provincial school inspector or other appropriate educational authority.
Overseas, teachers are obtained for D.N.D. schools overseas on a loan of service basis from their employing Canadian schools boards. The boards continue to pay their salaries in accordance with the salary schedule in effect and applicable to the teachers' qualifications and experience. The Department of National Defence reimburses the school boards for such salary payments.
Free quarters are provided to the teachers overseas or allowances are paid in lieu if the teacher elects not to occupy such quarters. These allowances are payable overseas at rates approved from time to time by the treasury board.

subtopic: EXHAUST CONTROL DEVICES FOR MOTOR VEHICLES
EXHAUST CONTROL DEVICES FOR MOTOR VEHICLES
speechtext: Is consideration being given to following the example of California and promoting by law or by conference with the provinces the making mandatory of exhaust and crankcase control devices for motor vehicles?

speakerposition: Minister of Amateur Sport; Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: EXHAUST CONTROL DEVICES FOR MOTOR VEHICLES
speechtext:
Tested and approved crankcase control devices that reduce the motor vehicle contribution of air pollution by about 25 per cent to 30 per cent have been standard equipment on all new cars sold in California since 1962. Present standards require about a 70 per cent reduction in pollutants from auto exhaust.
The California state motor vehicle pollution control board have recently approved several exhaust control devices for installation on new cars sold in California beginning with 1966 models.
The United States automobile manufacturers association have promised to produce cars that will meet the California standards limiting exhaust contaminants for the 1967 model year.
In view of the above it is considered premature to promote a provincial conference on such devices until the equipment becomes available and satisfactory experience as to performance is forthcoming.

I was saying I hoped, in view of the discussions we had in committee, that it would not be necessary to make an additional statement. However, I accept the suggestion of the hon. member for Queens (Mr. MacLean).
The committee on marine and fisheries had a thorough discussion of the proposal in this bill for the establishment of a 12 mile fishing zone, and agreed with its provisions that the government be given the necessary power to establish straight base lines.


In the committee I indicated that it was the intention of the government, when this bill was passed by parliament, to establish without delay the fishing zones of Canada, and I indicated that this might be done by bringing into effect those portions of the bill relating to fishing, while deferring until a later date proclamation of the rest of the bill. After this testimony my colleagues and I considered the matter further, and subsequently the Minister of Fisheries stated on my behalf in the committee that the government did not expect any undue or substantial delay in bringing the entire bill into force. Therefore the situation is that there will be no delay in proclaiming the bill in its entirety after it has passed through the house and received royal assent.
I should like to take this opportunity to emphasize one or two points which my colleague and I mentioned in the standing committee. When the bill is proclaimed the immediate effect will be that the fishing zones of Canada will be established from existing base lines. These base lines will follow mainly the sinuosities of our coast line, pending the drawing of straight base lines by the governor in council under clause 5 of the bill.
Those countries with which we are not having negotiations will therefore be immediately excluded from the fishing zones, and their vessels will be subject to penalties under the Coastal Fisheries Protection Act if they operate in those areas. This will be of great importance to Canada in view of the rapid development by certain countries of large, modern fishing fleets capable of operating very far from their home ports.
I would like to inform the committee that during the next few months we will be having another round of talks with a number of countries that are affected by the action we are taking. Negotiations with France and Britain will take place in July, and with others later in the summer and autumn.
In order to maintain the friendly atmosphere in which our negotiations with these countries have been taking place, and to facilitate their conclusion, we do not propose, as I have already informed the house, to interfere with the fishing of these particular states during this temporary period of our negotiations. When the bill is proclaimed the coastal fisheries protection regulations will be amended to allow the countries with which we are holding discussions to continue fishing pending conclusion of the negotiations, when final arrangements will come into effect.

The hon. member for Queens (Mr. MacLean), whose own experience in this matter is extensive and who has been very helpful in the discussions on this matter both in this chamber and in the committee, mentioned the need to table promptly in parliament all orders in council made under the proposed act, in particular orders made under clause 5, relating to the delineation of straight base lines. Such tabling is required by the Regulations Act, but even if it were not so required I would be glad to assure the committee that every order in council made under this bill will be tabled in parliament without delay. I mentioned this matter privately to the hon. gentleman, I believe yesterday, and he raised a certain point. I find that the situation is as I have stated, and I do not believe he need have any concern in that regard.
This bill will have implications not only for Canadians now living but for future generations. It means a great deal to the fishing communities in our country. I would hope that this parliament would speak with one voice in the passage of this bill. In doing so parliament would be declaring to the world that the government, in taking this action is speaking for all parties in the House of Commons; and this, I am sure, would be a very important factor in the remaining portion of the negotiations upon which we will be embarking. I need not say anything more at this stage.
This bill will establish a 12 mile fishing zone in Canada. It will enable the government to establish the straight base line system. The straight base lines are not spelled out, for the reasons we gave in the committee, because this would interfere with the negotiations that are under way. This is following the practice established by other countries who have initiated new fishing zones based on the straight base line system, countries such as Norway and Iceland, and other countries I mentioned in the committee.
I commend this bill to the committee as being in the interests of Canadian fishermen and Canadian fisheries, and in the interests of Canada as a whole.

I wish to thank the Secretary of State for External Affairs for his statement. I might add that this bill has been carefully and thoroughly studied by the standing committee on marine and fisheries. Witnesses appeared before us representing various interests, and a very complete study of the measure was made.
Of course this legislation is a stage in a long process which has been going on for
8, 1964
Territorial Sea and Fishing Zones a number of years, the process of obtaining for Canada as far as possible exclusive rights for Canadian nationals in waters adjacent to our coasts. There is a difference of opinion on this, so I will not take up the time of the committee by restating arguments already made, but I personally think it is a great pity the legislation before us is not the culmination of this process. In my view the situation today would be more satisfactory if this could have been the case. I think the government now recognizes some of the stumbling blocks and difficulties which exist. It is not just a case of making some unilateral declaration which no other country is going to question, because other countries feel they have rights, and in any case they have means of retaliation should they wish to use them, if this question is not handled in a reasonably diplomatic fashion.
I believe the government is doing that. I am not criticizing the actions the government has taken, but I am criticizing the background which has been created and against which this bill is being introduced. I have no evidence to suggest that either of the two ministers who are now responsible were guilty in this regard, but a great many loose statements were made during the election campaigns to the effect that this was a simple matter; that all you had to do was make a proclamation and foreign fishing vessels would disappear. Indeed, it was suggested that the only reason this had not been done long since was that other governments, previous governments, were dilatory or did not take their responsibilities seriously. Of course anyone who is familiar with the situation knows that this is not the case.
I appreciate the generous remarks of the Secretary of State for External Affairs with regard to the efforts made by the previous government and by myself and other people in this connection. I should like, if I may, to digress for just a moment to pay tribute to the excellent work which has been done by the negotiators on behalf of Canada. I am thinking chiefly of senior civil servants, who have been an excellent negotiating team for Canada in this connection.
As I said earlier, I do not agree with the sequence of events. I would have hoped the government would not feel it was obliged to bring in legislation at a given time. I admit at once that this bill will have one helpful effect; that is, it will declare an exclusive fishing zone measured from our present base lines. But how much better it would have been if, before the end of May, as

Territorial Sea and Fishing Zones no doubt the government hoped, negotiations could have been completed to the stage where this legislation might have included the results of those negotiations so the minister could have made specific statements to parliament about what had been achieved. He could, for example, have told us what conditions had been agreed upon with regard to the tapering off period with respect to historic rights. A statement could have been made explaining precisely what the geographical co-ordinates were, and so on.
In this regard I should like to ask the minister a question which he may be able to answer later. I wish to refer to a news item which emanated from Washington last December. It reads as follows:
The Canadian government has surrendered a point upon which it strenuously insisted at the law of the sea conferences in Geneva in 1958 and 1960-that U.S. fishing rights within 12 miles of Canada's coasts cannot be maintained unlimited and in perpetuity.
Both external affairs minister Paul Martin and fisheries minister Hedard Robichaud said here yesterday that historic rights of U.S. fishermen will not be affected when Canada establishes a 12 mile national fishing zone, as it is proposed to do next mid-May.
I realize that some of this terminology may be loosely applied. I gather the government does not contemplate entering upon any negotiations to withdraw from or abrogate any treaty rights. But the report uses, I believe, the term "historic" in this case, and I should like to know whether the report is accurate when it says the government does not intend to negotiate with the United States on the question of historic fishing rights apart altogether from the treaty rights. Are these historic rights to remain permanent? That is a question I should like to have answered if at all possible.
This legislation, as has been said, is permissive for the most part. It does establish an exclusive fishing zone, but as far as the following are concerned, that is to say the establishment of the base lines, the geographical co-ordinates upon which the base lines are to be drawn, and the establishment of national waters by including them inside base lines

and I am referring here to bodies of water such as the gulf of St. Lawrence- this bill is only permissive. I hope the legislation will not, in these circumstances, become a ruse or a stratagem to have people believe that more progress has been made than has actually been accomplished.
What I am saying is that with regard to the latter points I have mentioned, the bill will have no effect at all until the negotiations

are complete. For my part I hope these negotiations can be successfully terminated without too great a delay. The Secretary of State for External Affairs and, I think, the Minister of Fisheries both told the house that this legislation would strengthen their hands in these negotiations. If that is true I support the legislation on that ground alone, as well as for some other reasons. But I think this is a debatable point. Perhaps its passage would weaken the hand of the negotiators; because when this bill is passed, and the negotiations are still not complete, all our people can do is continue to negotiate. On the other hand, if the legislation had not been passed our team could still say to representatives of other countries "If you are not going to be reasonable about this I am sure the Canadian parliament will declare unilaterally that we will take these rights".
This is, of course, a debatable point and a matter of opinion. I think we are all agreed that although technically we may be acting unilaterally as a result of taking action in parliament, in practice there is very little room to act unilaterally, at least in an arbitrary way. This is a world community as far as fishing is concerned, and we have to act in a way that will not be detrimental to us in dealing with our neighbours at the present time or in the future. However, I see very little difference between these negotiations and any previous negotiations dealing with world fisheries. In every other case-that I know of, in any event-the negotiations were completed, the agreement was signed and then it was ratified by the introduction of a bill which was passed by parliament. This would apply to the north Pacific treaty and to any other treaty you wish to name in connection with fisheries negotiations with other countries. I think this would have been a more logical way to approach this problem.
I recognize that this bill will do one thing; that is, it will proclaim an exclusive fishing zone based on our present base lines, and that has merit. But I think consideration should have been given to the introduction of a bill which included just that, plus a declaration that certain bodies of water, geographically described, were Canadian national waters and would not just become such by virtue of an order in council to be passed some time in the future. I think that would have been a neater, more decisive way of doing it.
But I am not going to quarrel about details. I think a great deal of hard work was done on this bill but, as I have already stated,

immediately the government came into power, it they did not know this before- and I think the two ministers concerned did know it-they should have known that this is not just a matter of a unilateral statement, even by legislation, which everyone is going to accept. For instance, at the meeting in Hyannis Port, according to the news report I read, the President of the United States reserved his position on this matter. At least one news report I read stated this. This meant that the United States had certain reservations in this connection. It is only natural that other countries will react in this way if they feel or suspect that their rights may be prejudiced.
I mentioned specifically the historic fishing rights position of the United States. I would like to have also, if it is possible, some statement with regard to what is contemplated in respect of the length of time historic fishing rights held by other countries are expected to be recognized; or is there going to be a phasing out process in this connection?
I want to thank the Secretary of State for External Affairs for mentioning the question of the tabling of the orders in council which will result. Like him, I also checked on the Regulations Act and found that, happily, the minister has no choice but to table them within 15 days of their being published in the Canada Gazette. That is a useful safeguard as far as parliament is concerned. But as I have already stated, I think from a legislative point of view the sort of blank cheque aspect of the powers that are granted the government with regard to the location of these geographical co-ordinates is bad legislation.
It is true that both ministers have said they do not expect to take action as a result of these powers which would be unreasonable, and so on; nevertheless the fact remains that there is no limitation on where these geographical co-ordinates can be placed. I think we should put some limitation on this, in the same way that on a cheque it is stated "Not good for more than $100". We should let the government fill in the exact amount, as it were, when they know what it is going to be. We do not expect at this juncture that the government is in a position to state exactly where these co-ordinates are going to be, but I think there should be in the legislation some limitation as to where they might be. I say that, Mr. Chairman, not in a critical way with regard to this govern-
Territorial Sea and Fishing Zones ment, but I am concerned with the principles of the matter. I think it is unwise for parliament to ever grant wider powers than those that are needed for the purpose in hand.
However, the drafters of this legislation have done a reasonably good job, I think. They have beon most ingenious in drafting what must have been a fluid bill, a bill that would do what was needed to be done at this juncture and would give permissive powers to do what remains to be done, and the minister might have suggested, too, that it should be made to look as if it is doing at least as much as it is doing, and preferably quite a bit more than it is actually doing.
I regret that with regard to the co-ordinates there is not some limitation which is more specific and which would have removed some doubts from the minds of interested parties, such as were mentioned by witnesses who appeared before the committee and expressed anxiety on the part of their clients that base lines might be drawn from the mainland of Nova Scotia to Sable island, thereby intersecting a well known international air corridor which passes over what are now the high seas, and as a result of this measure aircraft would be passing over what would be technical Canadian territory, which would subject them to the possibility of additional tolls and various other things that might occur in the future.
As the Secretary of State for External Affairs is aware, this party supports the principle of this bill in general terms. Had some slight changes been made in the details of the bill, which I have enumerated, and had the bill come as a crescendo at the end of these long years of negotiations, as a culmination of successful negotiations, we would have been able to support it wholeheartedly and without any reservations whatsoever.
I think it is rather unfortunate, at least from our point of view, that this is not the case. Nevertheless it is a step forward. There are negotiations yet to be carried out. I hope the minister is correct in his statement that this bill will strengthen his hand. We remember that only a year and a half ago, of course, they were the strong-armed people. They claimed they had all the strength needed. All the strength they needed then was to be elected and to form a government. I do not quarrel with that, but I hope the contention that it will strengthen their negotiating position is correct and that the results of this legislation will be as happy as we all hope.

Mr. Chairman, this bill has been reported back to the committee of the whole from the standing committee on marine and fisheries. I for one have no desire to attempt to duplicate in this debate that which was done in the standing committee on marine and fisheries. However, I think there are a few matters arising out of the proceedings of that committee which can properly be brought to the attention of this committee at this time.
Hon. members will recall that at the second reading stage of the bill we made clear by way of an amendment that we considered this a rather weak and futile bill to deal with a very important subject matter. While we are strongly in support of the general objective, we really do not consider the present bill to be a very satisfactory vehicle for dealing with this situation, either with regard to the terms of the bill or as to the timing of its introduction while negotiations are still in progress.
In the standing committee on marine and fisheries we sought to expand upon this position and to present some alternatives to the committee which we felt would better serve the purposes that I am sure all hon. members of the committee have in mind. It will be recalled that one of the points of difference -in fact, the hon. member for Queens (Mr. MacLean) made reference to it in the course of his remarks-is the question as to the manner in which the base line co-ordinates should be established. The Secretary of State for External Affairs and the Minister of Fisheries have indicated that the immediate effect of the bill is to establish a 12 mile fishing zone. In the committee I sought by way of amendment to propose what was in effect a compromise to the views which had become apparent as matters of difference on second reading by suggesting, in effect, that the committee should report back to the house the recommendation that the bill be separated; that we should then proceed immediately to enact a bill which would bring into effect a 12 mile fishing zone; and then at a later stage, when negotiations were completed and the government was in a position to tell us exactly what conclusions it had arrived at in its discussion with the other countries concerned, we could then enact a bill which would establish the co-ordinates in detail in respect to where the straight base lines would be established, which would clearly define which waters were being taken in to become part of the internal waters of Canada.


The majority of the standing committee did not see fit to support this proposal, and following failure of that proposal we took steps to put forward, at least for the record, our position in respect of this matter of establishing base lines by suggesting an amendment which would have clearly set out in the bill base lines which would have been established by sets of co-ordinates pretty well along the line of the base lines which were suggested in the submission of the fisheries council of Canada. However, there again the majority in the committee did not see fit to support such amendment, and while I realize it would be within my rights to introduce a similar amendment in the committee of the whole, I do not propose to do so because I think it would be a duplication of effort and really would not accomplish anything fruitful in view of the position which was taken in the standing committee.
While the hon. member for Queens (Mr. MacLean) voiced at least some objection to the proposals in the bill very similar to the objection which I expressed, I am rather regretful of the fact that he did not see fit to support my objection in a more direct and forthright manner than he did either on second reading stage or in the standing committee. I got the impression while listening to his earlier remarks that he was simply pointing out to the committee that during the time he was a member of the former government he and his government had perpetuated the position of the administration previous to them, which had consistently appeared to be afraid to grasp the nettle of this question. I may say I am happy that the present administration has moved at least one step toward grasping this nettle, and in that respect I commend its actions over and above that of the two preceding administrations, one of which was of course Conservative, the other being the former Liberal administration.
I have tried to make it clear right through the proceedings that parliament itself should, as far as I am concerned, be the body which establishes by clear and definite acts what will actually become the official boundaries of this country. In my view it is not appropriate, regardless of what the Secretary of State for External Affairs may say about the practice in other countries, that any body other than the parliament of this country should be the one which defines the boundaries of Canadian sovereignty. Changes in those boundaries should be brought about only as a result of direct action by the parliament of

Canada in a form which makes such action specifically part of the statutes of Canada.
About the time that the proceedings in the standing committee on marine and fisheries reached their conclusion some member in the house, during the course of a discussion about another matter, brought back to our attention a phrase which is becoming rather well known and is taken from a speech of the Prime Minister, in which he suggested that this is a time "to excite the daring". I should like to suggest, Mr. Chairman, that in the approach which has been taken to this matter, certainly as far as I have been able to see from the statements which have been made to us by the Secretary of State for External Affairs, his actions have been neither very exciting nor very daring. To come to the point which causes me to feel this, let me say at once it is because he has indicated more than once in the course of our discussions that he has no intention of raising with the United States in particular the question of the perpetuation of these old treaty rights. If I understand him correctly-and the hon. member for Queens (Mr. MacLean) raised this point-he has also indicated that he has no intention of discussing with the United States any revision or phasing out of their so-called historic fishing rights.
In the committee I tried to make it clear that our dealings with the United States should be on the basis of dealings with a good and friendly neighbour, but from any experience I have had in dealing with Americans as individuals I certainly feel that if there is one thing they understand it is straightforward and forthright dealings. I think we should have laid our cards on the table and have said we feel that these rather archaic treaty rights, which came into being at a time when we were not in a position to negotiate on our own behalf, should now go by the board. I think this would not be entirely a one-sided proposition.
I raised this question in the committee and the only answer I got from the Secretary of State for External Affairs was that it would not be in our national interest to do this. That is a flat declaration, but up until this time the minister has given us no indication whatsoever in what respect it would not be in our national interest. Quite frankly, I cannot help having some suspicion that what is happening is that our fishing interests are being sacrificed for some other unnamed and unspecified national interests, and I think this committee should be entitled to further information on which we can assess and judge

In other words, the original concessions which were granted by the United States to us had vanished while the United States had pretty well retained the original rights it received.

I was later informed that we still enjoy the right of free navigation of the Columbia from the international boundary to its mouth.
I bring this forward, not for any snide purpose by way of indicating that the minister does not yet know all the details regarding the subject of external affairs but to point out that I think it was a rather serious omission on the part of the Secretary of State for External Affairs, in opening these negotiations with the United States, that it did not occur to him that this might very well have been an important bargaining point in the discussions with the United States. I contend that this of itself provides a very valid reason for suggesting that there be some revision of existing treaty rights between our two countries.
While the suggestion I am now going to make may create a somewhat nostalgic reaction on the part of my colleague, the hon. member for Kootenay West, I do suggest quite seriously to the minister that when he renews negotiations with the United States he should raise this question and perhaps suggest to the United States that we would be willing to swap our rights of navigation on the Columbia for those old treaty fishing rights. I think he can do that nicely. I also think it might not be altogether amiss if it were to be pointed out to the United States that for practical purposes they have virtually abrogated the treaty provision with regard to our


right of navigation on the Columbia river without, as far as I am aware, ever discussing the matter with Canada. They did so when they built the original power dams across the Columbia. Those of us who live in the west know that there is no provision for ship navigation around Grand Coulee dam on the Columbia river.
I think that is the kind of approach that we as a free and sovereign nation should take. We are talking at least about having a distinctive flag and in my view we could very well point out to the United States that we want to sit down with them on a friendly basis and balance out a few of these things that have gone on in the past. Certainly we would not ask them to blast Grand Coulee dam out of the Columbia river at this stage of events in order to restore to us our treaty right to free passage on the Columbia. However, in exchange for our formally abrogating those rights we could very well request them to restore to us full sovereignty along sections of the Atlantic coast where under these old treaties they have rights which they must admit are not consistent with the full sovereignty of the Canadian nation.
I think this would put the whole situation in a context that would be a little more exciting, a little more daring, without making us obnoxious or antagonistic to our friends in the United States. Let us let them know this Canadian nation to the north is a nation which they should regard as a sovereign nation and which expects to be treated as equal even though it may not have as large a population as our cousins to the south have within their borders. This is the kind of approach I should like to see the Secretary of State for External Affairs take in his dealings with the United States. I think it could be presented in language which the people of the United States would understand. I feel the same thing should apply with regard to this matter of the claims to historic fishing rights and the negotiations on the phasing out period.
The hon. member for Queens (Mr. MacLean) suggested there is some question about whether or not this is going to be done. I certainly have a very clear impression that the Minister of Fisheries and the Secretary of State for External Affairs have told us they are not even going to raise this question of the phasing out of historic rights so far as the United States is concerned. Certainly, so far as the west coast of Canada is concerned it is abundantly clear the only nation that really has these so-called historic rights is the

United States. Unless we can come to some conclusion on this matter with the United States which provides for a phasing out, this whole action is more or less an exercise in futility so far as the improvement of the Canadian fisheries position is concerned.
This would not be a completely unprecedented action on our part. I happened to come across an article in a treaty between the United States and Great Britain in 1871. Article XVIII of that treaty provides for one of the forms of the renewal of the fishing rights of United States nationals in Canadian waters. Article XIX provides for reciprocal rights for Canadian fishermen in United States waters. It gives us those rights in terms fairly similar to those which were conferred upon the fishermen of the United States at that time. I should like to draw to the attention of the committee, Mr. Chairman, article XIX, and I quote briefly from it:
It Is agreed by the high contracting parties that British subjects shall have, in common with the citizens of the United States, the liberty, for the term of years mentioned in article XXXIII of this treaty, to take fish of every kind, except shell-fish, on the eastern seacoasts and shores of the United States north of the thirty ninth parallel of north latitude-
Now, article XXXIII of the treaty indicates that this right which is conferred by article XIX is to remain in effect for a period of ten years, and after that it will terminate. It seems to me, as I say, that this idea of a phasing out period is something which has been in existence in relation to the United States at least since 1871. I think it would not be out of place for us at this time to suggest to the United States that perhaps the thing be done in reverse to what it was in 1871. Certainly I hope before these negotiations are concluded that, in addition to the appropriate establishment of base lines we are going to have a clearcut understanding with the United States as well as with some of those other countries to which the minister referred, that we want this phasing out period; that we are not going to be satisfied in our negotiations until that has been achieved.
As I said earlier, Mr. Chairman, I have no desire to attempt to repeat in the committee of the whole house what took place in the standing committee on marine and fisheries. For that reason I am not going to take the time of the committee to attempt to reintroduce any of the amendments which I proposed in the standing committee on behalf of the New Democratic party. If the pattern of events is the same in committee of the whole as it was in the standing com-

I certainly am not going to oppose passage of the bill on third reading. In concluding I will agree with the hon. member for Queens (Mr. MacLean) by saying that, as far as it goes, it is a step in the right direction. This is something they had wanted for a considerable length of time, and I am sure it is something that should have been granted to them.
There are two or three main criticisms, and these have been referred to by other speakers. One was the failure of the government to specify the geographical coordinates. As has been pointed out by the Secretary of State for External Affairs this is something he feels would have interfered with the negotiations that are currently under way. The other main criticism, it seems to me, was the somewhat indefinite position in which we still find ourselves relevant to the existing fishing rights. These have been divided into two, the treaty rights and the

Territorial Sea and Fishing Zones historic fishing rights. I believe we were advised that so far as the treaty rights are concerned they are exercised to a very limited degree at present, and I am of the opinion that something could and should have been done with respect to renegotiation of these treaties. I shall be very brief, Mr. Chairman. I just want to say a few words to show where our party stands on this bill.
If I rise to speak on this matter, it is because I was one of my party's representatives on the committee on marine and fisheries and I am aware of all the discussions that took place there when that committee dealt with Bill No. S-17.
Now, I should like to point out that we are not altogether satisfied with the manner in which the Canadian fishing zone limits were set. We would have liked those zones to be much larger, but we understood the reasons given to us afterwards, according to which it is better to leave things as they are for the moment, while reserving the right to claim wider limits at the next opportunity.


I also believe that the legislation governing fish conservation which has been established and is in force in Canada is not adequately protected by this bill. In my opinion, the government should have been stricter and more to the point, if I may put it this way, when asking the other nations to observe the fishery regulations in effect in Canada, which is absolutely essential if our fisheries are to be preserved. After all, fisheries are a very important source of income for Canada and they should not be ruined. Therefore, legislation on conservation of Canadian fisheries must be enforced and we must forbid other nations to fish as they wish regardless of our legislation. We should be tougher in this field.
On the other hand, I would also have liked to see a firmer bill as far as historic and treaty rights are concerned. Canada should not take provocative steps towards other nations, but rather a firm attitude and indicate, first, through diplomatic channels, and then by firmer action, that these historical rights are more or less outdated and should not hinder the Canadian fishing trade.
It is with that in mind and also in order not to prolong this debate unnecessarily that we have decided to support Bill No. S-17, as drafted. As stated by the hon. member who spoke before me, we reserve the right to come back to this subject in a little while when the arrangements made by the government and the treaties entered upon between the government and other nations are known.
It is, therefore, with that in mind that, unanimously, we are going to vote in favour of the bill.

Howard Green, the former secretary of state for external affairs who did so much for this country, telling us of the efforts he had made to try to get agreement in the United Nations on an effective six and six mile formula. Why wait for 400 days? There must I presume have been negotiations throughout this period. If they now believe passage of this bill will strengthen

Territorial Sea and Fishing Zones their hands, why did they not bring it forward in the first 60 days so that their hands would have been strengthened during the past 340 days? It is hard for me to understand why they have waited so long.

Mr. Chairman, I want to discuss the aspects of this bill in the light of something which I think perhaps the minister and his advisers have completely overlooked in the consequential amendments that are set forth in part II of the bill. I discuss this question on clause 1 because the ramifications attendant upon the bringing into force of these consequential amendments cannot properly be confined to any particular clause of the bill in the committee discussion.
Part II of the bill, as the minister well knows, deals with some consequential amend-

merits and purports-I believe, without due notice to the public-to amend six acts. One of these is the Aeronautics Act, another is the Canada Shipping Act, as well as the Coastal Fisheries Protection Act, the Criminal Code, the Customs Act, and the Fisheries Act. I want to be specific about the Aeronautics Act, because I have given this matter some considerable study. In view of the very broad terms of clause 2 of Bill No. S-17, this singling out, as it were, of only the acts specifically named in part II of the bill must be-this is my conclusion, at any rate, and perhaps the minister can set me right if I am wrong- because this new bill, S-17, refers to "territorial sea" whereas the acts which are enumerated in part II of Bill No. S-17 refer to "territorial waters", "Canadian waters", "three nautical miles", "waters of Canada", and like expressions. These expressions are used respectively in the acts specifically set out in part II of the bill. I refer to the acts which are being consequentially amended.
If the acts listed in part II are required to be amended consequentially; if it is necessary that they be amended consequentially, then I would submit to the minister and his advisers that there are many other Canadian statutes-and statutes implementing treaties, incidentally-as well as treaties themselves, to which Canada is at least a signatory, which would also require amendment.
I am going to give just one or two very brief examples. Again, Mr. Chairman, these are examples with which I am familiar. The first one I would like to put to the minister is the bill that is, or was, before the other place. I am not sure whether it is still before the Senate. I refer to Bill No. S-25, an act respecting the Geneva conventions, 1949. The minister will note that in article 91 at page 78 of Bill No. S-25, in paragraph 3 the expression "territorial waters" is used. Why should not this treaty be amended, if the Aeronautics Act, which also refers to "territorial waters", is being amended? This argument applies also to the other five specific statutes set out in part II of Bill No. S-17. The only answer I can conclude as being correct is that one cannot very easily amend a treaty that Canada has already signed.

The minister says this is the point. Then this seems to be very inconsistent, since there are many other treaties to which Canada is a signatory, and which may or may not have become law in Canada by an act of parliament, which refer to "territorial waters".
Territorial Sea and Fishing Zones A further example is section 2 of article VIII of the convention on international civil aviation, 1944, signed by Canada. This is commonly called the Chicago treaty. I would like to read from a copy of that treaty which I have in my hand, for the benefit of the minister and so it will be on the record. I shall read section 2 of article VIII, which sets forth:
For the purposes of this agreement the territory of a state-
And Canada is one such state:
-shall be deemed to be the land areas and territorial waters adjacent thereto under the sovereignty, suzerainty, protection or mandate of such state.
Again, Mr. Chairman, the minister will note that the expression "territorial waters" is used. This seems to be directly in conflict with the proposed amendments to the Aeronautics Act which Bill No. S-17 attempts to bring about by part II. I would be very interested in the explanation of the minister's advisers, or the Minister of Justice, as he is in the chamber, on this very point. I see that the Minister of Justice is leaving the chamber, perhaps the point is not nice enough. It was under the Chicago treaty, that I have mentioned, that the international civil aviation organization, as the minister knows, was set up with offices and headquarters in Montreal. It seems to me that unless this bill, to be consistent, goes on to amend by an act of parliament these other treaties to which Canada is a signatory, what we are doing is bringing about the application of the breaking of a treaty. That is the only conclusion to which I can come. Perhaps the minister has a logical explanation for this, and if he has I would be very glad to hear it.
Another statute, with which I am sure the minister is familiar, is the Admiralty Act, which is to be found in the Revised Statutes of Canada, 1952, volume 1, chapter 1. In section 18(1) this act adopts the law of England. In the law of England the expression which is and has been long established is "territorial waters" or "three mile limit". Why has the Admiralty Act not been amended, as well as many other acts and treaties in which the expression "territorial waters" or similar expressions are used? Does clause 2 of Bill No. S-17-to put the specific question to the minister-cover this situation? Does clause 2, or do any of the provisions of this bill, cover this situation? I cannot find how they do, but perhaps the minister can tell us whether the provisions of this bill affect the provisions

It would seem that if it is not covered in the bill, we are looking forward to a very sorry mess indeed in our admiralty law and jurisdiction.
With these few examples I am sure the minister can readily see that the action intended by Bill No. S-17-this is my view, at any rate-has not been fully thought out and studied as to all the repercussions it might have both internally and internationally. If the bill is allowed to stand in its present form, I am sure these repercussions will occur, particularly with regard to the Aeronautics Act; because of course the amendments that are purported to be made by part II consequentially affect all territorial air spaces above Canadian territorial waters, or territorial sea, which is the new expression that Bill No. S-17 uses.
In my view the wording of Bill No. S-17 would permit the establishment by order in council of dual, triple or multiple jurisdiction over these proposed new extensions to the well established international law covered by the expression "territorial waters" or "three mile limit", as for instance is used in the Admiralty Act. There could be one territorial sea for fishing, one territorial sea for shipping, and yet another territorial sea for aeronautics purposes. Under Bill No. S-17, "an act of state", to use that expression-and I use the expression in quotation marks-we will have the first Canadian unilateral acquisition of territory or parts of the sea by an act of state since confederation, except by specific agreement or by treaty, and Canada is setting, I feel-and this is my own personal, professional view-a bad example for the rest of the world. As an example-I am sure the minister will see the analogy-if Indonesia, using Canada's example as set forth in Bill S-17 as a precedent, did something similar the freedom of the sea and the air, and shipping and air flights, would all be cut off from the Pacific ocean to the Indian ocean. So you could draw similar analogies with any other state using Bill S-17 for a precedent with respect to treaties such as the Chicago treaty.
To my understanding of the expression "act of state", it means an act of aggression. It is an act of acquisition or a declaration of war against other states, and it is not to be entered into casually. I am being serious here. I do not mean to infer that Bill S-17 will cause any wars, but if the minister has referred to the specific definition of the ex-

pression "act of state" I think he will agree with me that such a unilateral act is an act of state if it abrogates any existing treaty. If such an act of state occurs, in essence it is action against another state. It is action which should not be entered into casually or without studying real necessities as opposed to all the possible dangers inherent in the taking of such action. It is, the minister will agree with me, a unilateral piece of legislation.
I do not think the minister has agreed, in regard to specific assurances from any other states that the action proposed in this bill is going to be accepted, not to confine this objection to fisheries but to broaden it and examine the effect it will have on international air traffic in the country. The further point can be made that the Statute of Westminster of 1931 might have given our country the right to legislate beyond its jurisdiction; but if so it must specifically repeal the law set out in the territorial waters act of England, which Canada has followed to date. In this connection I would refer the minister to the prefix to the statutes of Canada 1930, second session 1931, the 21st and 22nd years of George V, which sets out the power conferred on Canada. I see no such consequential amendment in part II to this bill which will alter that situation. I should like to quote very briefly from that prefix, to put it on the record:
No law and no provision of any law made after the commencement of this act by the parliament of a dominion shall be void or inoperative on the ground that it is repugnant to the law of England, or to the provisions if any existing or future act of parliament of the United Kingdom or to any order, rule or regulation made under such act, and the powers of the parliament of a dominion shall include the power to repeal or amend any such act, order or regulation, in so far as the same is part of the law of the dominion.
There is no doubt that the admiralty law of England applies in Canada. Section 18(1), which I have already quoted to the minister, says so. It says that the law of England includes the territorial waters act-that is, the three mile limit-and all other laws. Therefore, Canada has specifically to repeal those laws-and this is the nub of my point-if it is going to set up a new territorial sea. Canada must then establish a new set of laws to replace the admiralty law of England, to follow the matter out to a logical conclusion. The Admiralty Act of 1952, Revised Statutes of Canada, section 18(1), is in direct conflict, in my submission, with this present bill.
I am sure the minister can see, as can other members, that the question is indeed

involved, and that one simply cannot accept the statement that the six acts listed exhaust the acts of parliament which must be amended consequentially in order to implement the intention of the provisions of this bill. For instance, supposing under clause 2 that the governor in council selected Sable island as the geographical point as described therein from which to calculate base lines. The situation which would then arise would be that all of the territorial seas-and I see the minister is shaking his head, and I understood in committee that the assurance was given that this will not be done. But I do not think that this assurance is enough. While the minister probably has the assurances of his cabinet colleagues now, this in turn does not assure the people of the country of our international friends that some future government might not take action under clause 2 of this bill and use Sable island as a geographical point.
To conclude my example, if this were done and Sable island were so used it would mean that all the air space between Sable island and Halifax would become Canadian air space. If the amendments to what was Bill No. C-117 which was before the house last session to amend the Aeronautics Act- and this measure is again on the order paper this session-were to pass, every international carrier flying between New York and Prestwick would be subject to overflight charges; and I am sure that is not the result the minister wants. Strange as it may seem, the consequential amendments to the fisheries bill before us would have this very effect on the aeronautical activities of world aviation companies flying into, out of and near Canadian land, water and air space.

Mr. Chairman, in rising to speak on this measure I wish to state that I am in agreement with the basic principle of the bill. The bill states this in clause 2:
Every provision of this act extends and applies to every act of the parliament of Canada, now or hereafter passed, and to every order, rule or regulation thereunder, except in so far as any such provision is inconsistent with the intent or object of such act, order, rule or regulation, or would give to any word, expression or clause thereof an interpretation repugnant to the subject matter or context, or is, in any such act, order, rule or regulation, declared not applicable thereto.
In view of that statement, Mr. Chairman, I would refer to clause 12 of Bill No. S-17 where under subclause 3 of that clause section 31 of the Fisheries Act is repealed and the following substituted therefor:
No one shall leave any port or place in Canada to fish outside Canadian fisheries waters for fish the catching of which is at such time prohibited in the Canadian fisheries waters opposite to or nearest the place where such person proposes to fish, and no one shall bring into Canada any fish caught outside Canadian fisheries waters when fishing for such fish is prohibited inside the Canadian fisheries waters opposite or nearest to the place where such fish was caught, or shall bring into Canada any vessels, boats, nets, fishing gear, implements or appliances used in such fishing. '
In checking the original section in the Fisheries Act I find that the words "territorial waters of Canada" have been changed in the wording in the bill to read "Canadian fisheries waters". However, I believe this entire section should be amended as it discriminates against Canadian fishermen, and when we are dealing with the clause by clause study of the bill I intend to move an amendment.
I say it is discriminatory because at the present time the dragging of scallops is prohibited in two specific areas off the coast of

Territorial Sea and Fishing Zones Nova Scotia at certain times of the year. Under the fisheries regulations, which are designed to conserve the inshore fisheries, no person is permitted to fish for scallops within seven nautical miles of the counties of Annapolis and Digby from May 1 to August 31. The same law applies to Lunenburg county, where no person shall be permitted to fish for scallops within seven nautical miles of the coast of Lunenburg county between May 1 and October 31.
The Fisheries Act, in which section 31 is found, is dated 1932, and if this clause was enforced by the federal Department of Fisheries it would result in the Lunenburg county deep sea scallop fleet being tied up to the wharves each year from May 1 to October 31. It could also result in the curtailment of operations of any deep sea scallop dragger operating out of Annapolis and Digby counties from May 1 to August 31. In my opinion this is a form of discrimination against Canadian fishermen and Nova Scotia fishermen in particular.
Nova Scotia today is truly the scallop province of Canada, for our ships now account for at least 98 per cent of all Canadian scallop production. As a result of the Conservative government's shipbuilding assistance program, our fleet of scallop draggers has increased to 40 in the last three years, with more being launched every month. As might be expected, the catch per boat has declined as the fleet has increased in numbers, but despite this fact the scallop fishermen along the coast of Nova Scotia are still earning a good living through hard work at this particular type of deep sea fishery.
To give the committee some idea of the vast expansion which has taken place in this industry, I point out that in the year 1953 the entire catch of scallops in Nova Scotia amounted to a mere 1J million pounds, worth less than half a million dollars to the fishermen. In 1963 over 16 million pounds of scallops were landed, with a value in excess of $6 million to the fishermen, representing increases in both weight and value of well over 1,000 per cent in the short space of 10 years. With the Canadian market consuming less than one fifth of our annual scallop production, we are obliged to rely very heavily on the United States market. Even though the American fishing fleet has an annual production of some 25 million pounds, three quarters of which comes from the New Bedford, Massachusetts fleet there is still an annual scallop consumption in the United States of approximately 40 million pounds. This

gives the committee some idea of the terrific potential in this industry and, of course, our heavy exports of scallops help toward bringing our balance of payments in line with the United States.
In my opinion section 31 of the Fisheries Act, stating that fish are not to be caught outside territorial waters when catching is forbidden in territorial waters, may have had some value in 1932, but times have changed and the terrific growth in the deep sea scallop industry alone since 1953 would indicate that a change in the act is long overdue. The minister or his officials may point out that no one has been fined or had his fishing licence cancelled under this regulation. However, if it was enforced today the scallop fleet operating out of Lunenburg county could be legally tied up from May 1 until October 31, thereby creating untold financial hardship in this industry. In my opinion this section of the act not only discriminates against the scallop fishermen but also prevents the establishment of a deep sea lobster industry in Nova Scotia.
As most hon. members are aware, Nova Scotia is divided into lobster fishing zones and at the present time zones 6A and 6B, which lie between the high capes around the tip of Cape Breton island to point Michaud, are the only places in which lobsters may be legally caught up to July 15. Most of the other zones are closed on June 30. Zone 4 takes in an area from Cole Harbour in Guys-borough county along the south shore of Nova Scotia, which includes Halifax county, Lunenburg county, Queens, Shelburne, Yarmouth and Digby counties, and the fishermen are only permitted to catch lobsters in zone 4 from December 1 to May 31. During the remaining six months of the year lobsters cannot be caught and landed legally in this area, and this applies not only to lobsters caught on the inshore grounds but also to any lobsters that may be caught by a deep sea fisherman. Nova Scotia fishermen are thereby prohibited under clause 31 of the Fisheries Act of 1932 from exploiting a deep sea lobster fishery on Georges and Browns banks that could well be worth over $1 million per year in landed value to the fishermen.
In 1963 the landed value of all fish caught in Nova Scotia amounted to $35 million, which represents an increase of $12 million over 10 years ago. Of this total, an estimated 36 million pounds of lobsters brought in almost $18 million to our fishermen. Lobsters, therefore, are the greatest dollar earner for our

fishermen, with scallops in second place. However, in my opinion we are only scratching the surface of the lobster industry because due to prohibitive regulations we are not taking advantage of the opportunities offered by the deep sea lobster fishery. We know that a great market exists for lobsters both in North America and in Europe. Because of its economic importance, considerable interest is attached to this creature both by the fishing industry and the fisheries research scientists.
While much has been learned about this strange creature, there is still a lot more to be discovered. We know that lobster stocks occupy thousands of square miles of open coastal waters, and these could well be called our inshore lobster population. We also know that lobsters can be caught in our offshore waters from 100 to 200 fathoms deep in an area south of Georges bank approximately 100 miles from Yarmouth, Nova Scotia. What we do not know is the relation between these two lobster populations.
Some marine biologists claim there are actually two distinct lobster populations, while others claim that lobsters hatched in the deep waters offshore are carried by strong currents, while in the larvae or free swimming stage, and that these lobsters help to populate the inshore banks. Because of the efforts of the research ships located at the oceanographic base established at Bedford basin, Halifax county, by the previous Conservative administration, we are gradually learning more about the habits of the lobster and about the food and disease that affect both his growth and survival. Common sense tells us that it is wise to carry out conservation measures on our inshore lobster fishing grounds in order to assure relatively good catches and income to our lobster fishermen. However, I question the soundness of carrying out a conservation policy on deep sea lobsters which, in effect, applies only to any potential Canadian deep sea lobster fishermen, while leaving the grounds wide open to fishermen from any other nation wishing to exploit them.
This is what is happening under clause 31, which actually restricts Canadian fishermen from landing deep sea caught lobsters at any point in Nova Scotia for approximately six months of the year. However, while we are conserving the supply of large lobsters on Georges bank, there are at least a dozen United States deep sea lobster draggers operating out of Sandwich, Plymouth and New
Territorial Sea and Fishing Zones Bedford-Fairhaven, providing employment to approximately 75 fishermen.
According to the last bureau of commercial fisheries statistics in the United States, the offshore lobster fisheries were worth more than $1 million to New Bedford fishermen last year. In January of 1964, the catch of deep sea lobster draggers totalled 161,000 pounds with a landed value to the United States fishermen for that month in the vicinity of $94,000.
Now, these lobsters are large in size, with many of them ranging from 12 to 20 pounds in weight. This would indicate good feeding and growing conditions in that area of the ocean.

The New Democratic party, in line with important sections of the British Columbia fishing industry, has long made clear its desire to see the establishment of a Canadian fishing zone. Likewise, we have long made clear our very grave misgivings of the type of substitute for effective legislation which has been produced by the government in the legislation before us. It is a pretty "fishy" sort of substitute.
I feel that we want to see in Canada a "made in Canada" fishing zone bill which would assure a basis upon which Canadian fishermen and the Canadian fishing industry could operate in the knowledge that they would have the right to the fishing resources inside that area and not do as this legislation does, leave rights in perpetuity to other, non-Canadian powers. This is a principle we have put forward and which has been put

forward by many sections of the fishing industry in British Columbia. It is in line with the stand taken by several other nations which has imposed and established a similar fishing zone. We certainly concede it is necessary to negotiate with the other powers who have or claim to have historic rights or treaty rights which give their nationals a right to exploit Canadian fishing waters. However some of those treaties were signed on behalf of Canada more than a hundred years ago when, really, there was no Canada to negotiate for Canada.
Our opinion is that we should go ahead, as some other nations have done, establish our zone, then notify all other nations we are doing so and ask those who complain or object to come to us and negotiate on their own behalf. We think our prime interest is to establish a Canadian fishing zone for Canadians. This has been the policy of this party for years, both the C.C.F. and the New Democratic party. In 1963 and again in 1964, I personally moved Bill No. C-27 to establish a Canadian 12 mile fishing zone in line with the policy I have briefly outlined. This bill was talked out on both occasions. I might say that it was the same bill my colleague, the hon. member for Skeena, moved in this house in 1962. I think it is rather interesting, Mr. Chairman, to look back briefly at the discussion that took place at that time, as represented in Hansard, when the hon. member for Skeena moved his bill to amend the Coastal Fisheries Protection Act and establish a 12 mile fishing limit. This was in January, 1962, and had his bill been passed at that time it would have come into effect this month, in 1964. On rereading the text of that debate in Hansard I find there are two very brief quotations I would like to put on the record at this time.
As recorded at page 379 of Hansard for January 30, 1962, the hon. member for Skeena said:
In my opinion we should not sacrifice the interests of our fishermen any longer. We should not allow the attitude of the United States in this regard to influence us to the extent that we do nohing about this most important question.
As recorded at page 381 of Hansard of the same date the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate, who is now the Minister of Transport, said:
I should like to congratulate the hon. member for Skeena (Mr. Howard) both on the bill and on the very moderate and reasonable presentation he made of it. In saying that I am speaking for my party and I assert that we support the bill without reservation.

I am not very impressed by the dangers which it is suggested might arise from an attempt to enforce this. After all, if Iceland and Norway have been able to do this by unilateral action it is hard to persuade me that the Canadian people, if they had a resolute government which could make up its mind about anything, would have any difficulty in doing the same.

Territorial Sea and Fishing Zones an obvious injustice to the fishermen in Nova Scotia, the hon. member should not talk about it. This bill is not the type of legislation that the Canadian people expected. It is not the type of legislation that results from responsible government. The great problem is that this legislation, like so many of the things surrounding the promises made to the electorate in 1963, is another gimmick to say to the Canadian people: "We did what we told you we were going to do during the election campaign, even though it is not the same as what we described, but it is something more than you had when we took office."
There cannot be any strong opposition to this bill because there is not anything that is very objectionable about it, now that it has been presented to us. The only objection to it is that there is nothing very effective about it; there is nothing in it of great value to our fishermen.
The bill can stand a lot of improvement and we cannot achieve these improvements until more progress has been made in negotiations with the other countries concerned than has been the case up to date. I wish to say, Mr. Chairman, that I do not feel it would be possible to accept an amendment at this time, although I would like to consider this question and see the amendment before making a final commitment. But just the same, I wish to assure the hon. member now that my department is studying this very important matter which he has raised, and it is our intention, after giving it proper study and consideration, to make any such amendments that would be to the advantage of our own Canadian fishermen.
This is all I want to say at this time, Mr. Chairman, except that I would like to bring to the attention of the committee a correc-

tion to an error which was made in the minutes of proceedings and evidence, No. 4, of the standing committee on marine and fisheries in a statement made by Mr. D. F. Miller, president of the Fisheries Council of Canada. Mr. Miller is reported to have said:
Mr. Chairman, with your permission and before any questions are asked I should like to clear up one point.
Mr. Howard, in the debate on this bill in the House of Commons, and the brief from the united fishermen and allied workers union referred to this council as an "employees organization", or words to the effect.
Mr. Bernier here takes a strong exception to that implication, on behalf of the some 3,000 fishermen who make up Quebec united fishermen, a member organization of this council.
What Mr. Miller said, and his text is available to prove it, was that this council is an employers organization, not an "employees", as reported in the evidence.
In conclusion, I hope the committee will see fit to pass this bill, which will prove how important it is for the government to be given the enabling legislation. The government will proceed with the least possible delay to implement the bill. Only at noon today I received a report emanating from Vancouver to the effect that six or eight Russian trawlers were sighted fishing for groundfish in Hecate strait. We immediately asked for an investigation. The investigation is not altogether completed, but according to the information we now have those vessels which were sighted in Hecate strait could be coastguards from the navy checking for a plane which was lost in that particular area yesterday. However, we have had evidence at different times that U.S.S.R. trawlers have been operating off our shores, and as the Secretary of State for External Affairs and myself have stated since the debate on this bill commenced it is urgent that action be taken now. It may be that this bill will not meet the demands of the fishermen or of the fishing industry 100 per cent, but its imple-mention will improve the situation and give further assurance to the Canadian fishing industry.

Mr. Chairman, before the minister sits down is he in a position to clear up the question I asked regarding the position of the United States historic fishing rights? I am not speaking of treaty rights now. Are negotiations in progress to fix a date of termination for any of these historic rights which they claim? In other words, will there be a phasing out period, or is the United States totally unaffected by this bill except for

the fact that they are acquiescing in the principle of a 12 mile exclusive fishing zone as long as it does not affect them? Is that the position, or has the government been able to convince them that their historic rights should not go on indefinitely?

subtopic: LEGISLATION RESPECTING TERRITORIAL WATERS AND FISHERIES LAWS
speechtext:
I think the Secretary of State for External Affairs and myself have made it clear on different occasions that the historic rights of the fishermen from France and the United States would not be disturbed at this time. I should not say "at this time": they will not be disturbed by the application of this bill.
The hon. member referred to acquiescence. It is very important to Canada that we have the acquiescence of the United States to this bill. There will be another advantage which should be considered and not neglected, and that is the fact that we have made it known that this bill will be followed by certain changes in the Canadian fisheries regulations. If this bill is passed, when it is implemented certain changes will be made which will again give further protection to our fishermen; and we hope that the operations of United States and French fishermen will not be of the type which will discriminate against Canadian fishermen.

subtopic: LEGISLATION RESPECTING TERRITORIAL WATERS AND FISHERIES LAWS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I have a couple of questions on this clause with regard to the application of the Fisheries Act, which was under discussion on the first clause. Clause 4 states what the fishing zones of Canada will be, and says that the outer limit of a fishing zone is distant nine nautical miles from the nearest point of the inner limit line. To me this clause has an effect on the Fisheries Act. I hope I am not out of order, but when discussing an amendment to the appropriate section of the Fisheries Act it was argued that only the terminology was being changed. That would be true only if the territorial waters of Canada remained the same, which they will not; and it would be true only if the Fisheries Act applied to territorial waters. However, I think the Fisheries Act applies not only to the territorial waters but to the exclusive fishing zones. Therefore in my judgment this would have quite an effect on the application of the Fisheries Act. That is why, to my belief, the type of amendment 20220-332J
8, 1964
Territorial Sea and Fishing Zones suggested by the hon. member for Queens-Lunenburg is even more necessary, because the present regulations under the Fisheries Act have a much wider application by virtue of this clause than they had before, and therefore the consequences would be greater.
Another point the minister might be able to say something about-I think this is the appropriate place for me to raise it-is this. He mentioned that Russian trawlers were reported at this moment in the Hecate strait. The matter which concerns me in connection with the immediate effect of this bill after it is proclaimed is that it will not change the status of bodies of water like the gulf of St. Lawrence until the base lines are created from the geographical co-ordinates, unless of course the body of water concerned is less than 24 miles across. I know that when the bill is proclaimed it will have some effect by keeping foreign trawlers which have no historic rights 12 miles from the present base lines instead of three miles. But it will have no effect on these special bodies of water which we intend to proclaim national waters. I think we had evidence to this effect from experts, but perhaps the minister might have something to say on that point, although I do not want to hold things up.

subtopic: LEGISLATION RESPECTING TERRITORIAL WATERS AND FISHERIES LAWS
speechtext:
The hon. member referred to clause 4 which describes the fishing zones, and stated that it will have some effect on the application of some of the regulations made under the Fisheries Act. I am prepared to admit that, but what we have done in this bill, particularly in part II, is to make minor or consequential amendments having to do with the description of the territorial sea only.
Those are, as I have said, consequential amendments which had to be made. In so far as the Fisheries Act itself is concerned and the regulations under that act, I want to assure the hon. member that these matters are under consideration at present. It is quite obvious that certain changes will have to be made. As I have stated earlier, we have already studied the situation and we are prepared in the near future to make some changes affecting the operation of Canadian fishing vessels, particularly in those areas where we have a substantial inshore fishery. So I want to assure hon. members that this matter is at present under consideration.
