subtopic: LEGISLATION RESPECTING TERRITORIAL WATERS AND FISHERIES LAWS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, while I have no copy of the amendment I want to repeat what I have said before, that such an amendment is not in order and is not in line with the bill itself. It has been made very clear and it is a well known fact that legislation of this kind having to do with international problems is based on international law. Anyone who is familiar with the geography of the east coast of Nova Scotia will know that Sable island is over 100 miles from the mainland. The 40-odd countries which have taken or are taking a unilateral position have abided by the international practice, and I hope no one would wish to intimate that any government of this country would want to depart from this practice.
If we were to use Sable island as a coordinate it would create on the south coast of Nova Scotia a kind of triangle that would extend over 100 miles towards the high seas. When I was questioned about this matter in the committee it was made clear that Sable island, being Canadian territory and owned by Canada, will have its own fishing zone. It will be surrounded by a 12 mile fishing zone. It certainly would not be possible for Canada to apply the straight base line method, as mentioned in the bill, if we were going to use Sable island.
[The Deputy Chairman.]
So we certainly cannot support an amendment of this kind. I want to make it clear again that there is no need whatsoever for such an amendment because it departs entirely from the principle of the bill. It would create a precedent that could be followed by other countries and certainly would be questionable from the point of view of international practice. Therefore we cannot support the amendment.

subtopic: LEGISLATION RESPECTING TERRITORIAL WATERS AND FISHERIES LAWS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I think the very fact this amendment has been proposed indicates the rather foolish position into which the government has been drawn by the present terms of clause 5. If the government had done as we have been suggesting and had asked us to establish by act of parliament base line co-ordinates along the lines of the amendment which I attempted to propose in the standing committee, I think it would have been quite clear where we stood. The very fact that it is possible for an amendment of this kind to be brought in indicates one of the basic weaknesses of the present bill.
However, if we were to agree to spell out in the bill that Sable island would be excepted I think our position would be as foolish as the one the government has already taken in the matter of the establishment of the co-ordinates, and under the circumstances might very well be taken as an indication that while we were not going to go out into the ocean to pick Sable island as a co-ordinate it might be our intention to try to find some rock somewhere 100 miles off the west coast of Canada and use that. For that reason I do not feel I can support the amendment.

subtopic: LEGISLATION RESPECTING TERRITORIAL WATERS AND FISHERIES LAWS
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I agree with the statement made by the hon. member for Comox-Alberni. It seems rather strange to inject this one particular area into the bill. If we are going to designate certain areas for inclusion or exclusion it will open up the whole bill. Therefore I do not think the amendment is one that should be supported.

subtopic: LEGISLATION RESPECTING TERRITORIAL WATERS AND FISHERIES LAWS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I just want to say one word in a general way, particularly since the Minister of Justice is present. As far as I can see there is a tendency with regard to the legislation that the government is introducing, of which this is a perfect example, to ask in general terms for more power than is needed for what the government says it has in mind. This is the thing to which we object. As far as section 5 is concerned, whatever the intention of the government is the government will have the power to put one co-ordinate on Sable island,

another at Yarmouth and enclose that area. I am not saying for one moment this is their intention. The government has said it is not their intention. Why ask us to give them the power to do this if they are not going to use it? This is the point I am making. This sort of thing is extremely sloppy legislation. It is like someone saying, "We want you to sign a blank cheque because we want you to pay $13." Then, when you suggest that you put a limitation on the cheque, that it is not good for more than $25, they say, "No, trust us; we will not make the figure more than $13; just give us the blank cheque, anyway."
This is an authoritative attitude and seems to indicate they think that parliament can do no harm by giving them any amount of power.
I do not want to be unduly contentious about this thing, but it is bad legislation. I want to say that if the government keeps drafting legislation in this way it is inevitable they will run into objections not only in parliament but from people who fear they may be affected by it in a way far beyond the present intention of the government; that is our objection to the thing.

subtopic: LEGISLATION RESPECTING TERRITORIAL WATERS AND FISHERIES LAWS
speechtext: In view of the remarks just made by the hon. member for Queens (Mr. MacLean), I must say that I feel it would have been much more to the point if he and his colleagues had seen fit to support me in introducing in the committee a specific set of co-ordinates which referred to the east and west coasts of Canada. In so far as the east coast of Canada is concerned I named specifically 54 points from the terminal point of the United States-Canadian boundary on the south to a headland on the north. As I suggested, if we had been prepared to report to the house a specific suggestion along that line, then it would have been quite clear that neither the house nor the government in the future could have considered including Sable island as a co-ordinate.

The reason we did not support his amendment was that by moving such an amendment, in my judgment, we would be assuming the responsibility of the government. It is the government that must decide where these co-ordinates will be, based upon the advice and technical complications resulting from negotiations with other countries and so on. I want to support the hon. member entirely in his objective, but I do not think that is the way to achieve it. The

During the time copies are being made available may I say a few words on the amendment. I referred to the matter earlier when I replied to the remarks of the hon. member. This clause amends section 31 of the Fisheries Act and it is a consequential amendment having to do with the description of the term territorial waters and fisheries waters. It makes no change whatever in the present regulation in so far as it applies to the fishing operations of Canadian fishermen.
This is a provision which has been in the act since 1932 and, so far as I know, there has been no interfence with the operations of Canadian fishermen. But in view of the fact that the matter had been raised I put on the record earlier-and there is no need for me to repeat what I said before the committee-that it is our intention to review this particular clause of the bill, the application of which could probably be amended by a change in regulations.
It would not be fair to take a quick decision on a matter of such importance. The amendment reads "except under licence from the minister" and I ask what would happen if the minister decided to refuse such a licence? How would it improve the conditions of the Canadian fishermen? I agree that this is a matter which could be of grave concern to a number of fishermen operating on the east coast, particularly to any scallop or lobster fishermen who would want to operate in deep sea waters, but I cannot agree to the amendment in its present form.
Again I give the assurance that we will review the clause and we will take whatever action is necessary so that there will be no discrimination against any Canadian fisherman in this regard.
